gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's only above-rated output figure for the Elite 200 V2 (3,900 W 'Power Lifting') is limited by BLUETTI to 'pure resistive loads' like kettles and hair dryers. That means it is not a compressor-start surge. BLUETTI's US page publishes no surge figure at all, while Anker states '4,000W peak' with no duration.
standout_why: I compared against buyersheet.com (cited), generatorchecker.com (cited) and stationhours.com (#1 result). StationHours lists the Elite 200 V2 at '2,600 W / 3,900 W surge', so it counts Power Lifting as surge. BuyerSheet correctly says 'not published' but gives no reason. GeneratorChecker already says Power Lifting 'is designed for resistive loads' and that SurgePad may fall short for motor starts, but it says this only for the AC200L and C1000, not the Elite 200 V2, and it gives no surge durations. So rivals already have part of the finding (the boost-mode caveat). The new part is that the Elite 200 V2's 3,900 W is not a surge figure and BLUETTI publishes none. None of the pages gives a surge duration for any model.
decides: It confirms the pick rather than changing it. Every candidate's continuous rating (2,400 to 2,600 W) is already above the 1,300 W (StationHours) to 2,100 W (BuyerSheet) start-up spike these pages assume for a 5,000 BTU unit. So on the maker pages I could open, no candidate needs its boost or peak figure to start the compressor. For the table this means: compare stations on continuous watts, mark the Elite 200 V2 surge as 'not published (3,900 W is resistive-only Power Lifting)', and write Anker's 4,000 W as 'peak, duration not stated'. Don't add the Elite 200 V2's 3,900 W to a surge column the way StationHours does.
